knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,

options(warn = 1)

::: {.callout-note}
**Key functions**

- Before solving: `check_feasibility()`, `validate_scenario_parameters()`,
  `process_operability()`, `audit_coefficients()`.
- Diagnose infeasibility: `multimod::lp_bounds()`.
- Verify results: `verify_solution()`, `compare_solve_settings()`.
:::

A model can fail in two ways. It can fail loudly: the solver returns
INFEASIBLE, and nothing in the solver log names the row that cannot be met. Or
it can fail quietly: the solve returns OPTIMAL, but a missing value was
replaced by a default, a process could never run, or the matrix carries
coefficients the solver had to scale away. energyRt has a check for each stage
of the model life cycle, and most of them need no solver at all.

| Stage | Check | What it finds |
|---|---|---|
| Declared model | `check_feasibility()`, `interpolate_model(check = TRUE)` | forced requirements above ceilings that cannot be raised |
| Interpolated scenario | `validate_scenario_parameters()` | missing, duplicated or out-of-domain parameter rows; storages and corridors without their governing equations |
| | `process_operability()` | processes that cannot operate in a region and year, and why |
| | `audit_coefficients()` | the coefficient range of each equation family |
| Infeasible solve | dummy import / export on commodity balances | which balance cannot close, where and when |
| | `multimod::lp_bounds()` | matrix rows whose activity range misses their bounds |
| Solved scenario | `verify_solution()` | accounting identities recomputed from the solution |
| | `compare_solve_settings()` | disagreement between backends or storage settings |

This article walks through each check on a small model with one planted defect
per stage. Every block runs on the bundled GLPK in a few seconds.

```{r setup}
library(energyRt)

debug_project <- file.path(tempdir(), "debugging")
set_scenarios_path(path = debug_project)
set_models_path(path = file.path(debug_project, "models"))
set_repositories_path(path = file.path(debug_project, "repositories"))
set_registry_file(path = file.path(debug_project, "energyRt_registry.csv"))

annual_timetable <- make_timetable(struct = list(ANNUAL = "ANNUAL"))

annual <- newCalendar(
  name = "annual",
  timetable = annual_timetable
)

horizon_2030 <- newHorizon(period = 2030)
```

Energy is measured in PJ and costs in MEUR. With `cap2act = 1`, one unit of
capacity produces 1 PJ per year.

# Before interpolation: contradictions in the declarations

Some infeasibilities are visible in the data before any decision is made: a
demand larger than everything that can ever supply its commodity, or a stock
of capacity that consumes an auxiliary commodity the model cannot provide.
`check_feasibility()` compares such forced requirements with ceilings that no
decision can raise, per commodity, region and year. In the model below the
only source of electricity is a supply capped at 6, against a demand of 10.

```{r feasibility, message = TRUE}
ELC <- newCommodity(
  name = "ELC",
  desc = "Electricity",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "PJ"
)

SUPELC <- newSupply(
  name = "SUPELC",
  desc = "Electricity supply with a fixed ceiling",
  commodity = "ELC",
  unit = "PJ",
  supply = data.frame(
    cost = 1,
    ava.up = 6
  )
)

DEMELC <- newDemand(
  name = "DEMELC",
  desc = "Electricity demand",
  commodity = "ELC",
  unit = "PJ",
  demand = data.frame(demand = 10)
)

short_repo <- newRepository(
  name = "short_repo",
  ELC,
  SUPELC,
  DEMELC
)

short <- newModel(
  name = "short",
  desc = "Supply ceiling below demand",
  region = "R1",
  horizon = horizon_2030,
  calendar = annual,
  discount = 0.05,
  repo = short_repo
)

check_feasibility(object = short)
```

The finding lists the requirement, the ceiling, the shortfall and the object
that forces it. A declaration without a region applies to every region of the
model, and one without a year to every year, which the table shows as `NA`.
The same check runs inside `interpolate_model()` with `check = TRUE`, which
then stops instead of building a scenario that would only come back
INFEASIBLE:

```{r feasibility-interp, message = TRUE, error = TRUE}
SHORT <- interpolate_model(
  object = short,
  name = "SHORT",
  check = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

A clean result does not mean the model is feasible. Everything that depends on
a decision -- whether capacity can serve the load, whether a bound binds,
whether dispatch closes in every timeslice -- is left to the solver.

# After interpolation: parameters, operability and coefficients

The running example from here on converts gas to electricity. The combined
cycle plant has 5 units of standing capacity and is capped at 5; an open-cycle
plant is declared but capped at zero; demand is 10.

```{r model}
GAS <- newCommodity(
  name = "GAS",
  desc = "Natural gas",
  timeframe = "ANNUAL",
  unit = "PJ"
)

SUPGAS <- newSupply(
  name = "SUPGAS",
  desc = "Natural gas supply",
  commodity = "GAS",
  unit = "PJ",
  supply = data.frame(cost = 1)
)

CCGT <- newTechnology(
  name = "CCGT",
  desc = "Combined-cycle gas power plant",
  input = list(comm = "GAS"),
  output = list(comm = "ELC"),
  cap2act = 1,
  ceff = data.frame(
    comm = "GAS",
    cinp2use = 2
  ),
  capacity = data.frame(
    stock = 5,
    cap.up = 5
  ),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 100)
)

OCGT <- newTechnology(
  name = "OCGT",
  desc = "Open-cycle gas power plant",
  input = list(comm = "GAS"),
  output = list(comm = "ELC"),
  cap2act = 1,
  ceff = data.frame(
    comm = "GAS",
    cinp2use = 3
  ),
  capacity = data.frame(cap.up = 0),
  invcost = data.frame(invcost = 50)
)

toy_repo <- newRepository(
  name = "toy_repo",
  GAS,
  ELC,
  SUPGAS,
  CCGT,
  OCGT,
  DEMELC
)

toy <- newModel(
  name = "toy",
  desc = "Gas-to-power model with a capacity cap",
  region = "R1",
  horizon = horizon_2030,
  calendar = annual,
  discount = 0.05,
  repo = toy_repo
)

BASE <- interpolate_model(
  object = toy,
  name = "BASE",
  verbose = FALSE
)
```

## Parameter consistency

`interpolate_model()` validates the interpolated parameters by default
(`validate = TRUE`) and warns about advisory findings. The same checks can be
run again on any scenario to collect the findings as a table: index columns
without values, duplicated keys, parameter rows outside their maps, maps not
covered by their parameters (a value the solver would silently replace by its
default), and objects whose flows lack their governing equations -- a storage
without its balance chain or a corridor without its capacity link, either of
which would supply a balance without limit and still solve to OPTIMAL.

```{r validate}
base_findings <- validate_scenario_parameters(
  object = BASE,
  action = "silent"
)

base_findings
```

The toy scenario has no findings of this kind.

## Processes that cannot operate

A process can be declared and still be unable to run: its input has no source
in the region, it has no capacity and no investment window, or a bound fixes
its capacity, availability or activity at zero. `process_operability()` lists
such processes and the reason.

```{r operability}
process_operability(object = BASE)
```

Limits that act through the solution, such as an emission cap or a tax, are
outside this check.

## Coefficient ranges

Wide coefficient ranges come from unit choices -- a capacity in MW against an
hourly activity share, a ramp divided by a timeslice share -- and make a solver
work harder or stop with a numerical failure. `audit_coefficients()` writes
the scenario, reads the matrix back and summarises the non-zero coefficients
per equation family, with the variable families at each end of the widest row.

```{r audit}
audit_coefficients(x = BASE)
```

# An infeasible solve

None of the checks above finds the planted defect: the plant that can serve
the load is capped at half of it, and the cap only bites once the model has to
dispatch. The solve stops with a warning and the scenario status records it.

```{r infeasible}
BASE <- solve_scenario(
  object = BASE,
  solver = solver_options$glpk,
  verbose = FALSE
)

BASE@status$optimal
```

## Dummy import and export on commodity balances

The model has a built-in slack on every commodity balance: a dummy import that
adds the commodity and a dummy export that removes it, each at a price per
unit. Both are off by default. They are switched on through the `debug`
argument of `newModel()`, a table with one row per commodity, region, year and
timeslice; `NA` in any of these columns stands for all of them, and an
infinite price keeps that side off.

```{r slack}
dummy_prices <- data.frame(
  comm = NA_character_,
  region = NA_character_,
  year = NA_integer_,
  timeslice = NA_character_,
  dummyImport = 1e3,
  dummyExport = 1e3
)

toy_slack <- newModel(
  name = "toy_slack",
  desc = "Gas-to-power model with dummy import and export",
  region = "R1",
  horizon = horizon_2030,
  calendar = annual,
  discount = 0.05,
  debug = dummy_prices,
  repo = toy_repo
)

SLACK <- interpolate_model(
  object = toy_slack,
  name = "SLACK",
  verbose = FALSE
)

SLACK <- solve_scenario(
  object = SLACK,
  solver = solver_options$glpk,
  verbose = FALSE
)

SLACK@status$optimal
```

With the slack the model solves, and the slack variables show which balance
could not close and by how much:

```{r slack-result}
dummy_import <- getData(
  object = SLACK,
  name = "vDummyImport",
  merge = TRUE
)

knitr::kable(
  x = dummy_import,
  caption = "Dummy import, PJ"
)
```

Electricity in 2030 is short by 5: the gap between the demand and the capped
plant. No dummy export is used. `summary()` reports the total cost of the
slack, so a non-zero value is visible without querying the variables:

```{r slack-summary}
summary(object = SLACK)
```

The price should be well above every real cost in the model, so that the
slack is used only where nothing else can close the balance. The slack does
not cover user constraints (`newConstraint()`) or a bound that contradicts
another bound; a model that stays infeasible with the slack on every
commodity is infeasible for one of those reasons.

## The matrix: implied bounds

The direct-matrix route of the [multimod](https://github.com/optimal2050/multimod)
package builds the same linear programme without a solver.
`multimod::lp_bounds()` propagates the row and column bounds to a fixed point
and lists the rows whose possible activity cannot reach their bounds.

```{r lp-bounds, eval = requireNamespace("multimod", quietly = TRUE), results = "hide"}
toy_mm <- multimod_from_energyRt(
  object = BASE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

toy_lp <- multimod::model_to_lp(model = toy_mm)

toy_bounds <- multimod::lp_bounds(lp = toy_lp)
```

```{r lp-bounds-rows, eval = requireNamespace("multimod", quietly = TRUE)}
infeasible_rows <- toy_bounds$bounds$infeasible

toy_lp$row_index[infeasible_rows, ]
```

The flagged rows are the electricity output totals of region `R1` in 2030: the
output that the capped plant can deliver does not reach what the balance
requires. Propagation is row by row, so it finds conflicts that a single
equation decides; a contradiction that only arises from several equations
together passes it and is left to the dummy slack or to the solver.

# After a solve: accounting identities

A solve that returns OPTIMAL can still carry a defect in the solver, the model
template, the writer or the reader. `verify_solution()` recomputes the core
identities -- the commodity balance and its sign, the source and sink totals,
the cost decomposition and the discounted objective -- from the solution
tables and reports any row that does not close.

```{r verify}
slack_verified <- verify_solution(object = SLACK)

slack_verified$ok

print(
  x = slack_verified,
  detail = "issues"
)
```

`verify_checks()` lists the available checks; `checks = "all"` adds the
costlier ones.

# Cross-checks between backends

The objective of a model does not depend on the backend or on how the
scenario is stored. Solving the same scenario with two backends, or with
different storage settings, separates a modelling problem from a backend
problem. `compare_solve_settings()` tabulates objective, time and status for
every combination and flags disagreement per solver.

```{r cross-check}
slack_compared <- compare_solve_settings(
  object = toy_slack,
  settings = list(default = list()),
  solvers = list(glpk = solver_options$glpk)
)

slack_compared$summary
```

Further solvers are added to the `solvers` list, for example
`solver_options$mm_highs` or `solver_options$julia_highs` where installed.

# A sequence for a failing model

1. `check_feasibility()` on the model, or `interpolate_model(check = TRUE)`.
2. The findings of `validate_scenario_parameters()` and
   `process_operability()` on the interpolated scenario.
3. For an INFEASIBLE solve: the dummy import and export on all commodities. A
   non-zero slack names the commodity, region, year and timeslice; a model
   that stays infeasible points to a user constraint or to conflicting bounds.
4. `multimod::lp_bounds()` on the matrix for the rows that cannot be met.
5. For an OPTIMAL but suspect solution: `verify_solution()`, then a second
   backend.
6. For numerical trouble (slow convergence, a solver that stops with a
   numerical status): `audit_coefficients()`.
